How we built the AssetHoard MCP server
AssetHoard's built-in MCP server lets Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf search your asset library and export into your game project. How we built it.

What is the AssetHoard MCP server?

It's a small server built into the AssetHoard desktop app that speaks the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open standard AI tools use to talk to other programs. When it's switched on, AI clients such as Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf and Claude Desktop can search your asset library, look at thumbnails, browse bundles, tags and projects, and copy assets into your game project. Optional write tools let them organise the library and import files too.
Which AI clients work with AssetHoard's MCP server?

Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf connect directly over HTTP using the setup snippet from Settings > MCP Server. Claude Desktop only launches local stdio servers, so for now it connects through the mcp-remote bridge, which needs Node.js.
Is the AssetHoard MCP server safe to leave running?

It's off by default and built to be boring from a security point of view. It only listens on 127.0.0.1, so nothing on your network can reach it. Every request needs a 48-character random token. Requests from web browsers are refused outright, which blocks DNS rebinding attacks. Write tools are a separate opt-in, imports need you to click Allow in the app, exports never overwrite files, and every change the assistant makes can be undone with Ctrl+Z.
Can an AI assistant delete my assets through MCP?

No. There are no tools for deleting assets or bundles. The only deletes are for categories nothing uses and projects that are already empty. Everything else the write tools do goes on AssetHoard's normal undo stack, labelled with MCP:, so you can reverse it.
Does AssetHoard need to be open for the MCP server to work?

Yes. The server runs inside the app, so close AssetHoard and the tools go away. That's deliberate: it means there's only ever one program writing to your library database, and the open window updates live when the assistant changes something.
Does the MCP server send my files to an AI company?

AssetHoard itself never sends anything off your machine. The assistant sees what the tools return: names, paths, tags, categories, metadata and small preview images. Your AI client then sends that to its model provider like any other context, so treat it the same way you'd treat pasting a file listing into a chat. Raw file contents are only copied into a folder you name, on your own disk.

You're three hours into building a level. You need a barrel. You know you own at least four barrel packs, because you bought them in three different bundle sales and one of them was "a steal". Finding them means leaving the editor, opening a file browser, and digging through folders called Downloads (2).

Meanwhile there's an AI assistant sitting in your editor that can write a state machine in eight seconds but has no idea what's on your hard drive.

AssetHoard is a local-first desktop asset manager for indie game developers and digital artists, and version 0.2.3 fixes that with a built-in MCP server. This post covers how we built it, why it's locked down the way it is, and the things we've found it genuinely useful for.

What MCP is, briefly

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for letting AI tools call other programs. A program exposes a set of named tools with typed arguments ("search", "export", "create_bundle"), and any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Claude Desktop) can discover and call them.

For an asset manager that's a natural fit. AssetHoard already knows every model, texture, sprite and sound you own, what's in which bundle, what it's tagged, and what each file depends on. MCP lets your assistant ask it.

The decisions that shaped it

Built into the app, not a separate program

The obvious shortcut would have been a little standalone server that opens AssetHoard's SQLite database and reads it directly. We didn't do that, for two reasons.

First, two programs writing to one SQLite file is how you end up with a corrupted library and a very bad afternoon. Second, the app would never find out about changes. You'd ask your assistant to tag forty rocks and the open window would keep showing them untagged until you restarted.

So the server runs inside AssetHoard itself, and the app has to be open for it to answer. That turned out to be a feature: every change the assistant makes shows up in the window straight away.

Living inside the app also means you stay in charge of it from the app:

  • Turn it on and off. One switch in Settings > MCP Server. It's off until you flip it, and a plug icon sits in the toolbar whenever it's running, so you're never guessing.
  • See what changed. When an assistant exports files or edits your library, AssetHoard shows a notification in the app saying what it did, and the settings page keeps a list of recent calls.
  • Decide how much the assistant can do. Out of the box it can only search, look and export. Changing your library needs "Allow write tools" switched on, and importing files pops up a prompt you have to approve. If you'd rather keep it read-only forever, just leave the write switch off.

One rule: MCP never touches the database directly

The MCP code lives in its own module, and it isn't allowed to call app commands or SQL. Everything goes through a small internal library API that sits underneath both the UI and the MCP server.

That sounds like bureaucracy, but it's what makes the write tools trustworthy. When an assistant moves an asset into a bundle, it runs exactly the same function as when you drag it there yourself. Same validation, same audit log, same undo entry. There's no second, slightly different code path quietly drifting out of sync with the real one.

It also makes adding a tool cheap. A new tool is a typed argument struct (whose doc comments become the descriptions the model reads) and a thin method that calls the library API. The interesting logic stays in one place and gets tested once.

Rust, rmcp and streamable HTTP

AssetHoard's backend is Rust, so we used rmcp, the official Rust SDK for MCP, with its streamable HTTP transport mounted on axum. Database work runs on blocking worker threads so a big search never stalls the app's async runtime, and each call is recorded in a recent-activity list you can watch in Settings.

We picked HTTP over stdio because the server lives inside a desktop app that's already running. Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code and Windsurf all connect to a local HTTP endpoint with a header, which is a one-line setup. Claude Desktop is the odd one out: it only launches stdio servers, so for now it connects through the mcp-remote bridge.

A fixed port, on purpose

The server listens on port 47823 by default. You can change it, but AssetHoard will never pick a different one on its own if that port is busy. Auto-switching sounds helpful until every client config you've written silently stops matching. Instead, a taken port shows up as an error with a readable message, and you choose what to do.

Making it safe to leave on

A local server that can read your files and write to your library deserves some paranoia. Here's what's in place:

  • Off by default. You turn it on in Settings > MCP Server.
  • Local only. It binds to 127.0.0.1, so nothing on your network or the internet can reach it.
  • Token required. Every request needs a bearer token: 48 random hex characters, compared in constant time. Regenerating it disconnects every client.
  • Browsers are refused. Any request with an Origin header is rejected, and the Host header must be a loopback address. Browsers always send Origin; CLI and IDE clients don't. This blocks DNS rebinding, where a malicious web page tries to talk to a server on your machine, and it's what the MCP spec asks local servers to do.
  • Write tools are a second opt-in. "Allow write tools" is a separate toggle, and it's checked on every call, so switching it off takes effect immediately, even for clients that are already connected.
  • No deleting your stuff. There are no tools for deleting assets or bundles. The only deletes are for categories nothing uses and projects that are already empty.
  • Exports never overwrite. If a file already exists at the destination, it's skipped and reported.
  • Imports ask first. When an assistant wants to import a folder, AssetHoard pops up a prompt with the path, file count, size and target bundle, and flashes the window. No answer within 60 seconds counts as no. If you trust your setup, "Import without asking" turns this off.
  • Everything is undoable. Writes go on the normal undo stack with an MCP: label, like MCP: Moved 1 asset into 'Rocks', and a toast tells you what changed. Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) works exactly as it does for your own edits.

A plug icon appears in the toolbar whenever the server is running, so you always know it's on.

Small things that made a big difference

Search returns text, thumbnails are separate. Search results are ids, names, types, paths and tags, which keeps them small. If the assistant wants to actually look at something, it calls get_thumbnail and gets a preview image of at most 256 pixels. That means it can check that the "mossy rock" really is mossy before suggesting it, without flooding its context with every result's picture.

Dependencies come along. Exporting a model brings its textures. Exporting a Godot .tres brings the files it references, and Unreal assets bring theirs. Exporting a whole bundle keeps its folder layout. Assets inside zip archives or .unitypackage files are pulled out first.

Clickable links. Every asset, bundle and project the server returns includes an assethoard:// link. The assistant can hand you a link, you click it, and AssetHoard jumps to that item. We added the link scheme to the app specifically for this.

Errors the model can read. An unknown id, a bundle inside a package, or write tools being switched off all come back as plain error messages rather than protocol failures, so the assistant can explain what happened or try something else.

What you can do with it

Here's what this looks like in practice. These are the kinds of things you'd type into Claude Code, Cursor or similar with AssetHoard running.

Set dressing without leaving the editor

"Find three different barrel models and a wood texture that matches, and copy them into Assets/Props."

The assistant searches your library, looks at the thumbnails of the best few, picks a set and exports them, textures included. You keep building the level. This was the main use case we designed for, and it's the one in the demo video.

Search by what it looks like, not what it's called

"Do I have any mossy stone wall textures?"

Search works the same way as AssetHoard's search bar: by name with typo tolerance, and by meaning when semantic search is turned on. Since 0.2.3 that includes embedded audio metadata too, so "glass shatter" can find SFX_0472_FINAL.wav if that's what its description says.

Narrow it down like you would in the app

"Show me Godot UI sprites from my Platformer Kit bundle."

Results can be filtered by file type, asset class, engine, tag, category or bundle. The assistant works out the bundle id itself and filters inside it.

Drop a whole tileset into a project

"Copy my 'Dungeon Tileset' bundle into the Godot project at C:/dev/crawler."

The bundle's sub-bundles become folders in the destination, so the structure you set up in AssetHoard carries over.

Tidy up the library (write tools on)

"Make a bundle called 'Rocks' under 'Environment', move every rock model into it and tag them 'nature'."

The assistant creates the bundle, searches, moves and tags. Each step appears live in the app and is its own undo entry. If it gets carried away and moves a boulder that was actually a potato, Ctrl+Z.

A slower but satisfying variation: "Find the untagged textures in my Downloads bundle, look at each one and suggest tags." Review the suggestions, say yes, and let it apply them.

Keep track of what a game uses

"Start a project called 'Crawler' and add the dungeon tileset and the footstep sounds to it."

Projects in AssetHoard only record references. Nothing moves, and an item can belong to several projects. Once a project is set up, you can ask questions like "list everything in Crawler and tell me which assets have no licence recorded", which is a much nicer way to find out before release than after.

Onboard a new pack

"Import C:/Users/me/Downloads/platformer-kit-v2 into my Platformer Kit bundle, then categorise the new assets by type."

AssetHoard asks you to allow the import, runs it through the normal import queue with the usual progress notification, then the assistant categorises what came in. The whole import is one undo entry.

What's next

The main gap right now is Claude Desktop needing the mcp-remote bridge. A small native shim that lets it connect directly is on the list. We'd also like to hear what you end up using the server for, because the tool list was shaped by our own workflow and yours is probably weirder.

Try it

The MCP server is in AssetHoard 0.2.3 and later. Open Settings > MCP Server, switch it on, and paste the setup command into your client. The MCP docs cover each client, and the tool reference lists every tool and its arguments. AssetHoard is free to download during the open beta, so the only thing it'll cost you is finally finding out how many barrel packs you own.

Why do solo indie developers lose motivation?

Solo indie developers usually lose motivation because of how long solo work is structured, not because they're lazy. The common causes are the long middle of a project where progress stops feeling visible, working in isolation with nobody to bounce off, comparing your day-one work to someone else's finished game, and burning out from treating rest as a reward you have to earn rather than part of the schedule. Motivation dips are a normal part of any long project, not a sign you've chosen the wrong one.
How do you push through a project when motivation runs out?

Stop relying on motivation and lean on habit instead. Set a small, non-negotiable daily minimum you can hit even on a bad day, shrink your tasks until the next step is obvious, and keep a visible record of what you've finished so progress stops being invisible. Motivation gets you started; systems keep you going once the novelty wears off.
Is it normal to want to quit an indie project halfway through?

Yes. The middle of a project is where the excitement of starting has faded and the reward of finishing is still far away, so almost everyone wants to quit there at least once. Wanting to quit is not the same as needing to. The developers who ship are rarely the most motivated ones. They're the ones who kept a steady pace through the part where it stopped being fun.
How do you avoid burnout as a solo game developer?

Treat burnout as a project risk and schedule against it. Build rest, sleep, exercise and time with people into your week instead of saving them as a reward for hard work, take at least one full day off the project each week, and stop at a set time most evenings. Burnout usually comes from long stretches of running flat out with no team to notice you're struggling, so watch for the early signs, like dreading opening the project or losing interest in ideas you used to love, and ease off before you crash rather than after.
How many hours a day should a solo indie developer work?

There's no single right number. Consistency matters far more than daily hours. A small daily minimum you can hit every day, even fifteen minutes or one commit, keeps a project moving better than occasional twelve-hour sprints followed by a week off. Pick a pace you could keep up for a year, set a stopping time, and let good days run longer on their own. If you're working around a day job, a few focused hours a week done steadily will still finish a game that's scoped to fit.
What tools help a solo indie developer stay productive?

The ones that remove friction, so the hours you do have go into the game rather than fighting your setup. A code editor you know inside out, a Git client that makes committing and rolling back painless, and an asset manager such as AssetHoard so you can find and preview the sprites, models and sounds you already own instead of digging through folders or buying them twice. Add a simple task list for keeping the next step small, and a playlist of banging tunes to get you into the zone. None of these make you motivated, but every bit of friction you remove makes it easier to start on a flat day.

Every solo dev I know has hit the same wall. The first few weeks of a project are electric. You can see the whole thing in your head, the ideas won't stop coming, and you'd happily skip meals to keep building. Then, somewhere around week six or month three, the electricity goes out. The work is still there. The excitement isn't.

This isn't a character flaw and it isn't a sign you picked the wrong project. It's the shape of every long piece of solo work. You will not feel motivated all the time, because nobody does. What you can do is build something that keeps you moving when the motivation is gone.

The short version

If you only take a few things away, take these. The rest of the post unpacks each one.

  • Stop waiting to feel motivated. Build habits that still produce something on a flat day.
  • Shrink the next task until it's almost embarrassingly small, then start there.
  • Set a daily minimum you can hit even on your worst day, and protect the streak.
  • Keep a visible record of what you've finished, on screen or on paper.
  • Beat isolation on purpose: find other devs, post devlogs, get one person to hold you to it.
  • Compare yourself to last month's you, never to someone else's finished game.
  • Treat rest, food, exercise and people as part of the schedule, not a reward you earn.

Motivation is a bad thing to depend on

Motivation is a feeling, and feelings come and go for reasons you don't control. You slept badly. The bug you spent all day on wasn't the real bug. Someone posted a screenshot of their game that made yours look like a student project. Any of those can flatten your drive for a day, and if your ability to work depends on feeling driven, you've just lost a day.

The developers who finish things have arranged their work so that a flat day still produces something. They've quietly stopped asking "do I feel like working" and started asking "what's the next small thing I said I'd do".

Shrink the task until it's stupidly small

When you can't face the work, the task in your head is almost always too big. "Build the inventory system" is not a task, it's a project, and staring at it does nothing but make you tired.

The fix is to shrink the next step until it's almost embarrassingly small. Not "build the inventory system" but "add one slot to the inventory grid". Not "do the audio pass" but "wire up the sound for the door opening". A task you can picture finishing in twenty minutes is a task you can start, and starting is the whole problem. Momentum almost always shows up once you're moving, it just refuses to show up beforehand.

On genuinely bad days, shrink it further. Open the project. Read the code you wrote yesterday. That's allowed to be the whole session. More often than not, once the file is open you'll fix one small thing, and one small thing is infinitely more than zero.

Set a daily minimum you can hit on your worst day

Pick a floor. Something so small that you'd feel silly not doing it even when you're exhausted or fed up. Fifteen minutes. One commit. One asset placed. One line of design doc.

The output barely matters. What the minimum protects is the streak. A chain of tiny days keeps the project alive in your head and stops the restart cost from piling up. If you skip a project for a fortnight, coming back costs you an afternoon just remembering where you were. If you touched it yesterday, you're already warm.

Some days you'll hit the minimum and stop, and that's fine. Plenty of days you'll hit the minimum and then keep going for two hours because you were never really tired, you were just staring at something too big. The minimum only has to get you to the desk. Most of the time, once you're there, you keep going.

Make progress visible, because your brain won't do it for you

The cruel thing about the middle of a project is that progress stops feeling like progress. The exciting, visible milestones are behind you and ahead of you, and the middle is a thousand small tasks that don't individually look like much. Left alone, your brain will happily conclude you've done nothing for a month.

So don't leave it alone. Keep a record it can't argue with. A "done" list you actually add to, a devlog you post every week whether or not anyone reads it, a folder of dated screenshots you can scroll back through. When the doubt shows up, you want evidence sitting right there. The version of your game from three months ago is the proof, and if you never captured it, the doubt wins by default.

None of this has to happen in front of a computer either. Grab a notebook and sketch the inventory system you've been putting off. Scribble down a world-building idea before it evaporates. Draw the level on graph paper. A page of notes from a walk is still a record of a day you moved the project forward, and some days it's the easiest kind to make.

This is one place a bit of tooling earns its keep. Being able to scroll back through what you've built, the sprites you've drawn, the models you've made, the packs you've assembled, is a quiet antidote to the feeling that you're standing still. Half the time you're much further along than it feels. (It's a big part of why I organise my asset library so I can actually see it.)

Isolation is the real enemy, not the work

The work is rarely what breaks people. Working entirely alone for months is what breaks people. No colleague to tell you the idea's good. Nobody to notice you shipped the thing. No standup where you say out loud what you did yesterday and quietly realise it was quite a lot.

You have to manufacture what a team gives you for free. Find a Discord of other solo devs (the AssetHoard Discord is one) and actually turn up in it. Post your devlog even to an audience of nine. Tell one friend what you're shipping this week so there's a human who'll ask how it went. Pair up with another dev and trade weekly check-ins. None of this is marketing. It keeps the work real to someone other than you. Externalising your progress to even one other person changes how the work feels, because suddenly you're not the only one who knows it exists.

If in-person is an option, take it. A monthly indie meetup or a game jam can reset your whole outlook in an afternoon, mostly by reminding you that everyone else is also stuck on something and doubting themselves too.

Stop comparing your middle to someone else's end

The screenshot that ruined your afternoon was a finished, polished, cherry-picked frame of someone else's months of unglamorous work. You compared it to your actual Tuesday, bugs and placeholder art and all. Of course you lost.

Everything you see online is a highlight. The trailer, the launch post, the "we hit a thousand wishlists" thread. You don't see the fortnight they spent fighting the same engine bug you're fighting, or the three redesigns they binned, or the week they didn't open the project at all. Comparison isn't just unkind to yourself, it's inaccurate, because you're missing most of the data.

The only honest comparison is you against you. Are you further along than last month? Then it's working.

Protect your life, not just your rest

A lot of solo devs treat rest as a reward they have to unlock by working hard enough, which means they never quite unlock it, which means they run flat out until they crash. Then they lose two weeks to burnout and call themselves lazy for it.

Rest isn't earned, it's part of the schedule. So is eating well, exercising, and spending time with friends and family. None of that is what you do once the real work is finished, it's the space that lets you recharge between sessions of the real work. Build it in on purpose. Take one full day off a week and don't touch the project. Stop at a set time most evenings. Go outside. The ideas that untangle your worst problems almost never arrive while you're grinding at the desk, they turn up in the shower, on a walk, doing the washing up. A rested brain is a faster brain, and a burned-out one ships nothing at all.

Burnout is not a badge. It's a project risk, and it's your job to manage it like any other.

What it actually takes

Staying motivated as a solo dev is mostly a matter of not needing to be motivated. You build small habits, you make your progress visible, you find a few humans to be accountable to, you rest before you're wrecked, and you keep comparing yourself only to yesterday's version of yourself.

Do that, and the flat days stop being a threat. They become just another Tuesday where you hit your minimum, close the laptop, and come back tomorrow. The people who finish games aren't superhuman. They just kept turning up through the boring middle, one small task at a time, until the finish line quietly showed up.

Keep turning up.
